derivation: First-principles analysis shows the statement fails on two grounds: (1) Identical predictions on a finite constraint set does not imply functional equivalence or reparameterization relationship ('rename'). Two fundamentally different networks (e.g., different widths) can both satisfy the same constraints without being renames of each other. (2) In the specific context of the solution space rigidity experiment, replacing candidates that make the same predictions would destroy the information needed to measure solution space dimensionality — the very objective of the experiment. The rigidity question hinges on whether multiple distinct solutions exist at a given capacity; replacing them conflates solution degeneracy with functional identity. Mathematically, if P_{c1}(x) ≈ P_{c2}(x) for x in constraint set, this only implies agreement on those points, not that c2 = φ(c1) for some reparameterization φ. The statement confuses empirical equivalence with structural identity.
key_assumption: The analysis assumes 'candidates' refers to distinct neural network configurations (different widths, initializations, architectures) and 'same numerical prediction' means identical outputs on the held-out constraint set within the 1e-3 tolerance specified in the experiment protocol.
